{{short description|Counts the number of necklaces of n colored beads picked from α available colors}}
In [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] mathematics, the '''necklace polynomial''', or '''Moreau's necklace-counting function,'''  introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Charles Paul Narcisse Moreau|first=C.|last=Moreau|year=1872}}, counts the number of distinct [[Necklace (combinatorics)|necklaces]] of <math>n</math> colored beads chosen out of <math>k</math> available colors, arranged in a cycle. Unlike the usual problem of [[Chromatic polynomial#Examples|graph coloring]], the necklaces are assumed to be aperiodic (not composed from a repeated subsequence), and counted up to rotation (rotating the beads around the necklace counts as the same necklace), but without flipping over (reversing the order of the beads counts as a different necklace). This counting function also describes the dimensions in a free Lie algebra and the number of irreducible polynomials over a finite field.

==Definition==
The necklace polynomials are a family of polynomials  <math>M_n(k)</math> in the variable <math>k</math> such that
:<math>k^n \ =\ \sum_{d\,|\,n} d \, M_d(k).</math>

By [[Möbius inversion]] they are given by
: <math> M_n(k) \ =\ {1\over n}\sum_{d\,|\,n}\mu\!\left({n \over d}\right)k^d,</math>
where <math>\mu</math> is the classic [[Möbius function]]. 

A closely related family, called the '''general necklace polynomial''' or '''general necklace-counting function''', is:
:<math>N_n(k)\ =\ \sum_{d\,|\,n} M_d(k)\ =\ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{d\,|\,n}\varphi\!\left({n \over d}\right)k^d,</math>
where <math>\varphi</math> is [[Euler's totient function]].

==Applications==
The necklace polynomials <math>M_n(k)</math> appear as:
* The number of [[Necklace (combinatorics)#aperiodic necklaces|aperiodic necklaces]] (or equivalently [[Lyndon word]]s), which are cyclic arrangements of <math>n</math> colored beads having <math>k</math> available colors. Two such necklaces are considered equal if they are related by a rotation (not considering reflections). ''Aperiodic'' refers to necklaces without [[rotational symmetry]], having ''<math>n</math>'' distinct rotations.  Correspondingly, <math>N_n(k)</math> gives the number of [[Necklace (combinatorics)|necklaces]] including the periodic ones: this is easily computed using [[Pólya enumeration theorem|Pólya theory]].
* The dimension of the degree ''<math>n</math>'' component of the [[free Lie algebra]] on ''<math>k</math>'' generators ("Witt's formula"<ref name="L7984">{{cite book | last=Lothaire | first=M. | authorlink=M. Lothaire | others=Perrin, D.; Reutenauer, C.; Berstel, J.; Pin, J. E.; Pirillo, G.; Foata, D.; Sakarovitch, J.; Simon, I.; Schützenberger, M. P.; Choffrut, C.; Cori, R.; Lyndon, Roger; Rota, Gian-Carlo. Foreword by Roger Lyndon | title=Combinatorics on words | edition=2nd | series=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and Its Applications | volume=17 | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=1997 | isbn=978-0-521-59924-5 | zbl=0874.20040 | mr = 1475463 | pages=79,84 }}</ref>), or equivalently the number of [[Hall set|Hall words]] of length ''<math>n</math>''. Correspondingly, <math>N_n(k)</math> should be the dimension of the degree ''<math>n</math>'' component of a free [[Jordan algebra]].
* The number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree ''<math>n</math>'' over a [[finite field]] with ''<math>k</math>'' elements (when <math>k=p^d</math> is a [[prime power]]). Correspondingly, <math>N_n(k)</math> is the number of polynomials which are [[Primary ideal|primary]] (a power of an irreducible).
* The exponent in the [[cyclotomic identity]]:  <math>\textstyle {1 \over 1-k z}\ =\  \prod_{j=1}^\infty\left({1 \over 1-z^j}\right)^{\! M_j(k)}  </math>.
Although these various types of objects are all counted by the same polynomial, their precise relationships remain unclear. For example, there is no canonical [[bijection]] between the irreducible polynomials and the Lyndon words.<ref>
Amy Glen, (2012) ''Combinatorics of Lyndon words'', [https://amyglen.files.wordpress.com/2012/03/melbourne_talk_feb2012.pdf Melbourne talk]
</ref> However, there is a non-canonical bijection as follows. For any degree ''<math>n</math>'' monic [[irreducible polynomial]] over a field ''<math>F</math>'' with <math>k=p^d</math> elements, its roots lie in a [[Galois extension]] field ''<math>L</math>'' with <math>k^n</math> elements. One may choose an element <math>x\in L</math> such that <math>\{x,\sigma x, ...,\sigma^{n-1} x\}</math> is an ''<math>F</math>''-basis for ''<math>L</math>'' (a [[normal basis]]), where ''σ'' is the [[Frobenius endomorphism|Frobenius automorphism]] <math>\sigma y = y^k</math>. Then the bijection can be defined by taking a necklace, viewed as an [[equivalence class]] of functions <math>f:\{1,...,n\}\rightarrow F</math>, to the irreducible polynomial<blockquote><math>\phi(T)=(T-y)(T-\sigma y)\cdots (T-\sigma^{n-1}y) \in F[T]</math>    for    <math>y=f(1)x+f(2)\sigma x+\cdots+f(n)\sigma^{n-1} x</math>.</blockquote>Different cyclic rearrangements of <math>f</math>, i.e. different representatives of the same necklace equivalence class, yield cyclic rearrangements of the factors of <math>\phi(T)</math>, so this correspondence is well-defined.<ref>
Adalbert Kerber, (1991) ''Algebraic Combinatorics Via Finite Group Actions'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=Fe7uAAAAMAAJ]
</ref>

==Relations between ''M'' and ''N''==
The polynomials for <math>M_n</math> and <math>N_n</math> are easily related in terms of [[Dirichlet convolution]] of arithmetic functions <math>\textstyle f(n)*g(n) = \sum_{d|n}f(n/d)\,g(d)</math>, regarding <math>k</math> as a constant.
* The formula for ''<math>M_n</math>'' gives <math> n\,M_n \,=\, \mu(n)*k^n</math>,
* The formula for ''<math>N_n</math>'' gives <math> n\,N_n \,=\,  \varphi(n)*k^n \,=\, n*\mu(n)*k^n</math>.
* Their relation gives  <math>N_n\,=\,1*M_n</math> or equivalently <math> n\,N_n \,=\, n*(n\,M_n)</math>, since the function <math>f(n)=n</math> is [[Completely multiplicative function#Properties|completely multiplicative]].

Any two of these imply the third, for example:
:<math>
n*\mu(n)*k^n \,=\, n\,N_n \,=\, n*(n\,M_n) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad  \mu(n)*k^n
= n\,M_n</math>
by cancellation in the [[Dirichlet algebra]].

==Examples==
: <math>
\begin{align}
M_n(1) & = 0 \text{ if }n>1 \\[6pt]
M_1(k) & = k \\[6pt]
M_2(k) & = \tfrac12 (k^2-k) \\[6pt]
M_3(k) & = \tfrac13 (k^3-k) \\[6pt]
M_4(k) & = \tfrac14 (k^4-k^2) \\[6pt]
M_5(k) & = \tfrac15(k^5-k) \\[6pt]
M_6(k) & = \tfrac16(k^6-k^3-k^2+k) \\[6pt]
M_p(k) & = \tfrac1p (k^{p}-k) & \text{ if }p\text{ is prime} \\[6pt]
M_{p^N}(k) & = \tfrac1{p^N}(k^{p^N}-k^{p^{N-1}}) & \text{ if }p\text{ is prime}
\end{align}
</math>

For <math>k=2</math>, starting with length zero, these form the [[integer sequence]]
:1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 30, 56, 99, 186, 335, ... {{OEIS|A001037}}

==Identities==
{{main | Necklace ring }}
The polynomials obey various combinatorial identities, given by Metropolis & Rota:
:<math>
M_n(k\ell, n) =\sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(i,j)=n} \gcd(i,j)M_i(k)M_j(\ell),
</math>
where "gcd" is [[greatest common divisor]] and "lcm" is [[least common multiple]].  More generally,

:<math>
M_n(k\ell\cdots m) 
=\sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(i,j,\ldots,r)=n} 
\gcd(i,j,\cdots,r)M_i(k)M_j(\ell)\cdots M_r(m),
</math>
which also implies:
:<math>
M_n(k^m) =\sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(j,m)=nm} \frac{j}{n} M_j(k).
</math>
